extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students and instructors in abstract algebra/module theory
extracted.subtask_description: Worked solutions and solution techniques for exercises in module theory (exact sequences, direct sums/limits, tensor products, flatness). Shows canonical constructions, diagram chases, and standard lemmas used to prove isomorphisms, exactness, and finite generation/presentation claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove module isomorphism by constructing inverse homomorphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: To show M ≅ L ⊕ N construct explicit maps φ : M → L ⊕ N and ψ : L ⊕ N → M and verify they are inverses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define φ(m) := ((π_L)m, (π_N)m) (or analogous maps given by idempotent components) and ψ(l,n) := s(l) + t(n) where s,t are the appropriate injections/section maps; check φψ = id and ψφ = id by evaluating compositions on generators and using the relations (e.g. π_iσ_j = δ_ij, σ_iπ_j + σ_jπ_i = 1 in the concrete instance). Also verify component equalities such as given projections/injections correspond under the isomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hom into a direct sum equals direct sum of Homs when domain finitely generated
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural injections Hom(N, M_i) → Hom(N, ⊕ M_i) induce an injection ⊕ Hom(N, M_i) → Hom(N, ⊕ M_i), and this is an isomorphism if N is finitely generated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show injectivity by noting a family of maps that sums to zero must be all zero (because each component map applied to any n gives almost-all-zero condition). For surjectivity when N is finitely generated, use generators n1,...,nk: the image of any f: N → ⊕ M_i lies in a finite direct subsum, so only finitely many components are nonzero, producing an element of the direct sum of Hom's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exact-sequence lemmas (Snake, Five, Nine) for diagram-chase conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Snake Lemma, Five Lemma, or Nine Lemma to commutative diagrams with exact rows/columns to deduce injectivity, surjectivity, or exactness of a middle morphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the hypothesis of each lemma carefully (which adjacent maps are injective/surjective). Example: Snake Lemma yields Ker/ Coker exact sequences to prove injectivity; Five Lemma: if maps in positions 3 and 1 are surjective and position 0 injective then middle map is surjective (and dually for injectivity); Nine Lemma relates exactness of first and third rows when columns are exact and the middle row is exact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove finite generation / finite presentation via short exact sequences and Schanuel-type arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use exact sequences and finite presentations to move finite generation/presentation along short exact sequences: e.g., if 0 → L → R^n → M → 0 and M finitely presented ⇔ L finitely generated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given presentations R^ℓ → R^m → M → 0 and an exact 0 → L → R^n → M → 0, apply Schanuel’s Lemma to relate L to a cokernel/image of a finite free module, yielding finite generation. Converse: use surjections from finite free modules onto submodules to build finite presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct counterexamples by explicit module constructions to test necessity of hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: When a naive statement is suspected false, build a concrete module (often an infinite direct sum of cyclic groups) demonstrating failure of a claimed equivalence (e.g., existence of a section alone does not guarantee a splitting isomorphism unless compatibilities hold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example in text: take an infinite direct sum of Z/⟨n⟩ components, choose a cyclic subgroup of order p inside a Z/⟨p^2⟩ component to show no retraction exists, yielding a short exact sequence that does not split despite a section existing abstractly; check induced maps on components to rule out retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate universal mapping property (UMP) to define/characterize (co)limits, free/projective objects, and tensor products
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the UMP to construct unique maps out of (or into) universal objects: direct limits, free modules, tensor products, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving an object is the direct limit, given compatible maps from the system to P define the unique map from the colimit by choosing an index containing each element and verifying well-definedness and linearity. For free/projective modules, lift basis images; for tensor products, factor bilinear maps through the tensor via UMP and use uniqueness to identify maps and isomorphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify pushouts as colimits and give concrete descriptions in Sets and R-mod
rubrics_metrics.description: Express the pushout of L → M and L → N as a direct limit and concretely as (M ⊔ N)/~ in Sets or (M ⊕ N)/Im(L → M ⊕ N) in R-mod.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model the pushout as the colimit over the 3-object category with two nonidentity arrows; in Sets take the disjoint union modulo the smallest relation relating images of elements of L; in R-mod take the direct sum modulo the image of L under (f,-g). Verify the universal property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filtered direct limits: express modules as directed unions of finitely generated submodules
rubrics_metrics.description: Every module is the filtered direct limit of its finitely generated submodules (and direct sums are filtered direct limits of finite direct subsums).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order the set of finitely generated submodules by inclusion (directed because sum contains both). Prove the union equals the module and check the UMP for the limit by defining maps on elements using an index containing that element, verifying well-definedness and linearity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute tensor products by constructing bilinear maps and using UMP (including base change)
rubrics_metrics.description: To compute or relate tensor products, write down explicit bilinear maps (e.g., multiplication map a × K → K) and use the UMP to factor and obtain canonical isomorphisms or surjections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for R domain with K = Frac(R) and nonzero submodule a ⊂ K, define multiplication map a × K → K, check bilinearity and universality to conclude a ⊗_R K ≅ K. For base-change, construct canonical map M ⊗_R N → M ⊗_{R'} N and identify its kernel as generated by (x' m) ⊗ n − m ⊗ (x' n); show surjectivity, and check conditions for isomorphism when R' is a quotient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate tensor products and quotients: (R/a) ⊗ M ≅ M/aM and (R/a) ⊗ (R/b) ≅ R/(a+b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tensoring with a quotient R/a yields the module modulo the action of the ideal: (R/a) ⊗ M ≅ M/aM; similarly for two quotients the tensor is the quotient by the sum of ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: View R/a as cokernel of a → R and use exactness properties (tensoring cokernel yields cokernel of tensored map) to identify images: a ⊗ M maps to aM in M, so cokernel is M/aM. Apply same reasoning to R/b to get R/(a+b). Note caution: a ⊗ M → M need not be injective in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functorial preservation criteria for finite sums, surjections, and cokernels (Watt-type statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear functor F : R-mod → R-mod preserves finite direct sums. The natural map M ⊗ F(R) → F(M) is surjective if F preserves surjections and M finitely generated; it is an isomorphism if F preserves cokernels and M is finitely presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use characterization of finite direct sum by maps to/from components and apply F to preserve those relations. For the canonical map analyze on finite generators or on a finite presentation and use exactness preservation hypotheses to deduce surjectivity or bijectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flatness inheritance and faithful flatness characterizations
rubrics_metrics.description: If R′ is a flat R-algebra and P is a flat R′-module then P is flat over R. Faithful flatness of R′ is equivalent to several conditions: ideals contract-from-extension, primes/maximals lift, and nonzero modules remain nonzero after tensoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tensor cancellation/isomorphisms (e.g., (– ⊗_R R′) ⊗_{R′} P ≅ – ⊗_R P) and exactness preservation to transfer flatness. For faithful flatness show equivalences: (1) injectivity of M → M ⊗ R′ for all M; (2) a = contraction of aR′; (3) primes contract; (4) every maximal extends to proper ideal; (5) M ⊗ R′ ≠ 0 for M ≠ 0. Prove the chain of implications as in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lifting/lifting-of-elements in filtered limits to test properties (e.g., domain, zero)
rubrics_metrics.description: To test properties of a filtered direct limit R = lim R_i, properties such as R = 0 or being a domain can be checked by lifting elements to some R_i and using the directed system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If R = 0 then 1 = 0 lifts to some R_j so R_j = 0. For domain: given x,y ∈ R with xy=0, lift x,y to some R_i and use directedness and transition maps to force one lift to be zero in some further R_j, hence x=0 or y=0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe cokernels/ kernels and limits interaction (cokernels commute with direct limits; kernels may not)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cokernels commute with direct limits (so lim Coker(f_i) = Coker(lim f_i)), but kernels need not commute, and a counterexample can be constructed using a diagram expressing cokernels as direct limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use that cokernel is a direct limit and limits commute (references to (6.8),(6.14) in text). To show kernels may fail to commute, build a system whose limit map has nonzero kernel while every stage has zero kernel (example using Z → Z → Z/2 diagram).
